properties.name: Veleia
properties.one_line: Trajan secured 1,044,000 sesterces in mortgage loans against 46 local estates here, and the 5% interest fed and educated 253 boys and 77 girls of the ager Veleias every month. The bronze tablet recording every loan and every pledged farm, turned up by ploughmen in 1747, is the largest inscribed bronze plaque to survive from the ancient world.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, 'The Purpose and Organisation of the Alimenta', PBSR 32 (1964)
R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Tabula alimentaria per un prestito ipotecario imperiale, da veleia, II secolo, 01.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Tabula Alimentaria of Veleia, Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Parma — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Circello
properties.one_line: Trajan lent roughly 400,000 sesterces to 51 landowners of this farming community in 101 CE, and the 5% interest fed 286 boys and girls of a population still known by the name of their Ligurian ancestors, deported here two centuries earlier. The bronze ledger recording every loan and every pledged farm was found at the community's forum near modern Circello.
sources: Museo Nazionale Romano — Terme di Diocleziano, Rome
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/The Arch of Trajan, Institutio Alimenta relief, Benevento, Italy - 49866556976.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Institutio Alimenta relief, Arch of Trajan, Benevento — Carole Raddato via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0

properties.name: Ferentino
properties.one_line: The senator Titus Pomponius Bassus, Trajan's first curator of the alimenta, personally set up the child-welfare fund in this Hernican hill town, and the citizens honored him with a bronze tablet of patronage. Ferentino's Roman terraces and gates, raised from massive polygonal blocks, still carry the town above the Via Casilina.
sources: CIL VI 1492 (Tabula patronatus of T. Pomponius Bassus)
properties.image_credit: Approach to the acropolis, Ferentino — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Como
properties.one_line: Pliny the Younger, grown rich in Rome but still Comum's most devoted son, deeded a farm to his hometown and leased it back for an annual payment that funded food and schooling for freeborn boys and girls, copying the mortgage method Trajan used for the state alimenta. He set out the whole arrangement, sums included, in a letter to a friend he was recruiting to do the same.
properties.image_credit: Lake Como from Narro — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Atina
properties.one_line: A local benefactor endowed Atina's own alimentary fund decades before Trajan expanded the program across Italy, and the town kept his memory in stone long after. Perched on a Volscian hilltop above the upper Liri valley, Atina's Roman circuit walls still ring the old acropolis.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)
properties.image_credit: Cathedral of Atina — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Mentana
properties.one_line: Nomentum sits on the short epigraphic list of Italian towns with a confirmed state alimenta fund, a Trajanic welfare grant layered onto a town already known for its wine and for Martial's country villa nearby. Little of Roman Nomentum shows above ground beneath the modern town of Mentana today.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, 'The Purpose and Organisation of the Alimenta', PBSR 32 (1964)
properties.image_credit: Mentana — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Pesaro
properties.one_line: Pisaurum, a Roman colony on the Adriatic coast road, is named among the Italian towns that ran a state alimenta scheme under Trajan, funded like every other town's by interest on mortgaged farmland. The colony's grid-planned Roman core still lies beneath the streets of central Pesaro.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)
properties.image_credit: Piazza del Popolo, Pesaro — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Saturnia
properties.one_line: Saturnia, an old Etruscan town built over sulfur springs in southern Tuscany, is recorded among the Italian communities that drew on Trajan's alimenta fund for its poorer children. Its Roman-era hot springs still cascade over travertine terraces just outside the walls today.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)
properties.image_credit: Cascate del Mulino thermal terraces, Saturnia — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Monteu da Po
properties.one_line: Industria, a river-port colony on the Po that traded in Alpine copper and iron, is counted among the towns with a documented Trajanic alimenta fund. Excavated foundations of its temple to Isis and Serapis, proof of the town's trade ties to Egypt, still stand in the fields outside modern Monteu da Po.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)
properties.image_credit: Aerial view of the Industria archaeological site — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Formia
properties.one_line: Formiae, a coastal stop on the Appian Way famous for its oyster beds and seaside villas, is documented among the Italian municipalities running Trajan's alimenta program. Cicero owned a villa here and was killed nearby in 43 BCE, a story every Roman visitor to the town already knew.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)
properties.image_credit: Formia at sunset from Castellonorato — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Capena
properties.one_line: Capena, a Faliscan town drawn early into Rome's orbit and known for its cult of the goddess Feronia, is named among the Italian communities running Trajan's alimenta program for poor children. The ancient town site lies a few kilometers from the modern hilltop settlement that still carries its name.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)
properties.image_credit: Street in Capena — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Cupramontana
properties.one_line: The children of Cupra Montana who drew Trajan's alimenta grants set up their own inscription honoring the emperor, calling themselves the 'pueri et puellae alimentari Cuprenses Montani.' The Picene hill town, still ringed by the vineyards that give its Verdicchio wine its name, sits above the Esino valley.
properties.image_credit: Verdicchio vines at Cupramontana — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Acqualagna
properties.one_line: Pitinum Mergens, a small hill town on the Via Flaminia in the Candigliano valley, appears in the alimenta record through an inscription once wrongly assigned to neighboring Urbinum before scholars reattributed it here. The Roman settlement's remains lie scattered through the countryside around modern Acqualagna, now better known for its truffles than its ruins.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Acqualagna veduta interna del Passo del Furlo.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Furlo Pass gorge near Acqualagna — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Subiaco
properties.one_line: An inscription raised by the 'pueri et puellae alimentarii' of Sublaqueum records a local branch of the child-welfare program in the Aniene valley above Rome, a town Nero had earlier dammed into a chain of ornamental lakes. The Roman dams that gave the town its name, sub lacu, 'below the lake,' still show along the riverbed today.
properties.image_credit: Subiaco, view toward the Sacro Speco — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Terracina
properties.one_line: The wealthy Tarracina native Caelia Macrina left the town 1,300,000 sesterces in her will: 300,000 for a new public building and 1,000,000 to fund monthly alimenta payments to 100 boys and 100 girls in memory of her son. Her private foundation began in the 150s CE, decades after this snapshot, though it followed a model Trajan had already made famous at Tarracina's neighboring towns.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Jupiter Anxur, Terracina — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Ephesus
properties.one_line: The Ephesian aristocrat Tiberius Claudius Aristion and his wife built this fountain between 102 and 114 CE, channeling water 210 stadia, roughly 24 miles, into a two-story marble facade with a statue of Trajan in the central niche. The building inscription dedicates it to Artemis of Ephesus, to Trajan, and to the city itself.
sources: IvE 424-425 (building inscription of the Nymphaeum Traiani)
properties.image_credit: Nymphaeum of Trajan, Ephesus — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Ephesus
properties.one_line: The equestrian financier Gaius Vibius Salutaris endowed a foundation of 21,500 denarii and 31 gold and silver statuettes in 104 CE, funding a procession that carried images of Artemis, the emperors, and the city itself from the Artemision to the theatre at every major festival. The 568-line inscription recording his gift once covered an entire theatre wall and is now in the British Museum.
sources: G. M. Rogers, The Sacred Identity of Ephesos: Foundation Myths of a Roman City (1991)
properties.image_credit: Great Theatre of Ephesus — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Citta di Castello
properties.one_line: Pliny the Younger, patron and native benefactor of Tifernum Tiberinum, paid for a temple at his own expense and wrote to Trajan asking permission to add a statue of the deified Nerva beside the older emperors already displayed inside it. His letters describe choosing the site and commissioning the work in his own words.
properties.image_credit: Cathedral facade, Città di Castello — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Cassino
properties.one_line: Ummidia Quadratilla paid for an amphitheater seating 4,500 people and a temple in her hometown of Casinum, and the inscription she left behind names only the gift, not a reason. Pliny the Younger wrote up her death in 107 without once mentioning either building, too busy being scandalized by her private troupe of pantomime dancers. Her amphitheater still rises from the hillside above the old Via Latina.
properties.image_credit: Roman theatre in the Casinum archaeological park, Cassino — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Leptis Magna
properties.one_line: The Punic merchant Annobal Tapapius Rufus paid for Lepcis Magna's market out of his own pocket in 8 BCE, raising two stone tholoi ringed by forty shop counters where traders once weighed grain, oil, and purple dye. His dedication was cut in Latin above a Neo-Punic translation, announcing the gift in both languages his city actually spoke. The market still stands beside the old harbor road, one of the best-preserved Roman marketplaces anywhere.
properties.image_credit: Market (Macellum) of Leptis Magna — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Ephesus
properties.one_line: Gaius Sextilius Pollio built Ephesus a fountain in 97 CE at the edge of what became Domitian Square, drawing water through an aqueduct that carried his own name across the hills. His foster son finished the monument after his death, turning it into a family shrine with statues of Pollio and his wife Ofillia Bassa standing in its niches. The arched facade still frames the approach to the city's State Agora.
properties.image_credit: Pollio Fountain, Ephesus — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Cartama
properties.one_line: Iunia Rustica, Cartima's first priestess for life, rebuilt the town's collapsing porticoes, paid off its public taxes, and donated the land for a new bathhouse, all at her own expense. She then added a private portico beside those baths with a fish pond and a statue of Cupid, and threw a public banquet the day it opened. The town council answered by voting her a bronze statue in the forum, a rare civic honor for a woman anywhere in the Roman West.
properties.image_credit: Hilltop of Cartama, site of Roman Cartima — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Sagalassos
properties.one_line: Claudia Severa and her brothers Tiberius Claudius Aquila and Tiberius Claudius Pius, the richest family in Sagalassos, financed the city's first monumental fountain house around 100 CE, an apsidal marble facade wrapped in an Ionic colonnade greeting travelers entering from the south. It was the first fountain at Sagalassos actually built to move water rather than just to flatter an emperor's name. The family's gift stood at the north end of the Lower Agora for a full century before Severan builders dismantled and rebuilt it.
sources: Sagalassos Archaeological Research Project excavation reports
properties.image_credit: Sagalassos archaeological site — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Ephesus
properties.one_line: Gaius Julius Aquila built Ephesus a library to hold his father's remains and 12,000 scrolls, raising a two-story marble facade lined with statues personifying Wisdom, Virtue, Knowledge, and Judgment. His father, Tiberius Julius Celsus Polemaeanus, had governed the province of Asia and asked to be buried inside the very building his fortune paid for. Construction began around 110 CE and the facade stood finished by the time Trajan died in 117, one of the only libraries in the Roman world doubling as a tomb.
properties.image_credit: Library of Celsus, Ephesus — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Aphrodisias
properties.one_line: The freed slave Gaius Julius Zoilos returned to his hometown of Aphrodisias a wealthy man and paid for the theater's stage building, part of the Temple of Aphrodite, and the north colonnade of the agora. Julius Caesar had freed him and given him Roman citizenship, and Augustus later wrote to the city that he still liked his old friend Zoilos. Reliefs from Zoilos's own tomb monument, unearthed in 1956, now fill a room in the Aphrodisias museum.
properties.image_credit: Reliefs from the tomb monument of Gaius Julius Zoilos, Aphrodisias Museum — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Herculaneum
properties.one_line: Marcus Nonius Balbus paid for Herculaneum's basilica, its main gate, and a stretch of the city wall, all recorded in one blunt inscription: his name, his office, and the phrase 'with his own money.' The town council answered with at least ten statues of him scattered across the streets and a terrace with its own altar raised in his honor. Vesuvius buried every one of his gifts under volcanic material in 79 CE, and archaeologists are still pulling his statues out of the hardened ash.
properties.image_credit: Statue of Marcus Nonius Balbus, Herculaneum — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Ancient Corinth
properties.one_line: Gnaeus Babbius Philinus rose from a freedman's son to duumvir of Corinth, and along the way built the city a small round marble monument on the forum's west side entirely at his own expense. His own inscription records that he approved his own gift in his official capacity as duumvir, then went ahead and built it anyway. The monument's circular base still marks the edge of the Roman forum at ancient Corinth today.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of the Roman forum, Ancient Corinth — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Pompeii
properties.one_line: Eumachia, Pompeii's public priestess and patron of the fullers' guild, built the largest structure on the forum's east side, a covered hall and colonnaded courtyard dedicated to Augustan Concord and Piety. She paid for it in her own name and her son's, and the fullers who used the building set up a statue of her inside in gratitude. Vesuvius buried the hall in 79 CE, but its marble doorway and dedication inscription survived intact under the ash.
properties.image_credit: Statue of Eumachia, from her building at Pompeii — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Pompeii
properties.one_line: Marcus Tullius, three times duumvir of Pompeii, donated both the land and the money to build the city's Temple of Fortuna Augusta at a busy crossroads north of the forum. His dedication inscription lists his whole career, ending with the title 'military tribune by the people's request,' an honor Augustus reserved for men he wanted promoted into the equestrian order. The temple's podium and altar still stand at the corner of the Via della Fortuna.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Fortuna Augusta, Pompeii — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Pompeii
properties.one_line: The brothers Marcus Holconius Rufus and Marcus Holconius Celer rebuilt Pompeii's Large Theatre around 2 BCE at their own expense, adding a vaulted crypt, box seats, and new stone seating for the entire cavea. Two identical inscriptions, each over six meters long, run across the stage building recording the gift in nearly the same words. Rufus kept a reserved double seat in the theater for the rest of his life, its outline still cut into the front row.
properties.image_credit: Large Theatre, Pompeii — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Munigua
properties.one_line: Lucius Valerius Firmus served twice as duumvir of Munigua and paid for a temple, the forum itself, its porticoes, an exedra, and the town's archive building, all recorded on two matching bronze plaques. His gift helped turn a Baetican hill town into home to the largest terraced sanctuary built anywhere outside Italy, modeled on the great sanctuary of Fortuna at Praeneste. Munigua's stepped terraces still climb the hillside above the valley of the Guadalquivir's tributaries.
properties.modern_location: Villanueva del Rio y Minas, Spain
properties.image_credit: Terrace sanctuary of Munigua — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Cereatae Marianae
properties.one_line: This small Latin town in the upper Liri valley is attested as an alimenta community through an inscription in which its alimentary boys and girls dedicated a monument to Hadrian, found alongside a separate sacred dedication to Apollo in the same excavation. The find shows Trajan's welfare program still running here a generation after he founded it.
properties.modern_location: Casamari, comune of Veroli, Frosinone, Italy
sources: M. R. Picuti, Un'iscrizione sacra ad Apollo, una dedica dei pueri et puellae alimentari all'imperatore Adriano..., Atti del V Convegno epigrafico cominese (2009)

properties.name: Sestinum
properties.one_line: This small Umbrian hill town on the upper Foglia river is attested as an alimenta beneficiary through a dedication its alimentary boys and girls set up to Antoninus Pius in 161. The date, the very year of that emperor's death, shows Trajan's loan scheme still paying out roughly sixty years after it began.

properties.name: Tifernum Mataurense
properties.one_line: On the upper Metauro river, this small municipium is attested as an alimenta town through a dedication its alimentary boys and girls set up to Hadrian. It sits in a tight cluster of small Regio VI towns along the upper Tiber-Metauro watershed with unusually dense alimenta epigraphy.
properties.modern_location: Sant'Angelo in Vado, Province of Pesaro e Urbino, Italy
sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities, Alimentarii Pueri et Puellae

properties.name: Asisium
properties.one_line: This Umbrian town's alimentary boys and girls honored a local magistrate for administering the emperor's welfare payments to them, a rare piece of evidence for how the alimenta was run day to day rather than just how it was financed.
sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities, Alimentarii Pueri et Puellae

properties.name: Ficulea
properties.one_line: This old Latin town on the Via Nomentana, only 15 kilometers from Rome, is attested as an alimenta beneficiary through a dedication its alimentary boys and girls set up to Marcus Aurelius. It is one of the latest-dated pieces of alimenta epigraphy, showing the institution still running decades after Trajan founded it, right at the edge of Rome's own suburbs.
properties.modern_location: Tor Lupara, comune of Fonte Nuova, Italy

properties.name: Urbinum Mataurense
properties.one_line: This is the likely identification of a Metauro-valley town whose alimentary boys and girls dedicated a monument to Antoninus Pius, grouped by scholars with the nearby Sestinum and Tifernum Mataurense dedications from the same regional cluster. The identification with modern Urbino, rather than a separate unlocated town of a similar name, is the standard scholarly reading rather than a certainty.
properties.modern_location: Urbino, Province of Pesaro e Urbino, Italy

properties.name: Calvi Risorta
properties.one_line: Cales joined the roster of Latin colonies whose landowners took out Trajan's alimenta mortgages, pledging farmland around the old Via Latina town to seed a fund for the district's poor children. The 5 percent interest on those loans, the same rate fixed at Veleia and the Ligures Baebiani, was paid out every month as food money for boys and girls whose families could not otherwise feed them. Long before the welfare scheme arrived, Cales had already given Rome one of its favorite exports: a coarse black-glaze pottery so common in Republican-era shipwrecks that archaeologists still call the ware 'Calenian.'
sources: Greg Woolf, 'Food, Poverty and Patronage: The Significance of the Epigraphy of the Roman Alimentary Schemes in Early Imperial Italy,' Papers of the British School at Rome 58 (1990), pp. 197-228

properties.name: Como
properties.one_line: The senator and letter-writer Pliny the Younger built his hometown a public library around 97 CE at his own expense, then endowed it with 100,000 sesterces for its permanent upkeep. He separately gave 500,000 sesterces to support the town's freeborn boys and girls, and left Comum public baths in his will along with 300,000 sesterces to furnish them. A monumental inscription once mounted above the baths listed the full record of his gifts to the city.
sources: CIL V 5262 (Comum benefaction inscription, known from a 15th-century copy and one surviving fragment)
properties.image_credit: Statue of Pliny the Younger, Como Cathedral facade — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Bursa
properties.one_line: The orator Dio Chrysostom rebuilt the center of his native Prusa with a new colonnaded stoa and library between about 100 and 112 CE, demolishing older structures along the route to make way for it. He placed a statue of Trajan inside the library and entombed his own wife and son in a monument at the center of the colonnade. The project provoked a formal inquiry after rivals accused him of destroying the city's older buildings without authorization, a dispute Pliny the Younger investigated in person as governor of Bithynia around 111 CE.
properties.image_credit: Roman sculpture, Bursa Archaeological Museum · Wikimedia Commons (reused, same site as mint_prusa_ad_olympum)

properties.name: Saelices
properties.one_line: The local notable Proculus Spantamicus paid to pave Segobriga's newly built forum around 15 BCE, laying limestone slabs across the square and setting his own name into the pavement in gilded bronze letters. The dedication ranks among the longest bronze-letter pavement inscriptions known from a Roman Spanish forum. The square he financed remained the civic center of the town for the rest of its Roman history, still standing complete in 117 CE.
sources: Segobriga forum pavement inscription (Proculus Spantamicus dedication in bronze letters)
P. Pensabene, R. Mar & R. Cebrian, 'Funding of public buildings and calculation of the costs of the stone materials: the case of the Forum of Segobriga' (Tarragona, 2012)
properties.image_credit: Forum cryptoporticus, Segobriga — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Leptis Magna
properties.one_line: The Punic magistrate Annobal Tapapius Rufus paid for Lepcis Magna's stone theatre out of his own funds in 1-2 CE, giving the city its first permanent venue for plays and public assemblies. He recorded the gift in matching Latin and Neo-Punic inscriptions cut above the entrance arches, the same bilingual formula he used a few years earlier on the city's market. The theatre, its seating built partly into the hillside behind a colonnaded stage building, still stands today.
sources: IRT 321-322 (Latin building inscriptions of Annobal Rufus)
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre, Leptis Magna — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Pozzuoli
properties.one_line: The wealthy merchant Lucius Calpurnius built Puteoli's Temple of Augustus at his own expense in the early 1st century CE, raising a Corinthian temple with nine fluted columns down each flank and a white marble cella. His dedication survives cut into the architrave, recording that he built the temple and its ornamentation at his own cost. The temple's walls still stand today, later absorbed into the town's cathedral.
sources: CIL X 1613 (dedicatory inscription of L. Calpurnius)
CIL X 1614 (architect's inscription, L. Cocceius Auctus)
properties.image_credit: Pozzuoli Cathedral, built into the Temple of Augustus — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Ephesus
properties.one_line: Two freedmen of the imperial household, Mazaeus and Mithridates, paid for the triple-arched south gate of Ephesus's commercial agora in 4/3 BCE. They dedicated it to their former owners — Augustus, Livia, Agrippa and Julia — in a bilingual Latin and Greek text running the full width of the facade. Two ex-slaves thereby signed the busiest doorway in the city. The gate still opened onto the agora in 117 CE.
sources: Bilingual Latin/Greek dedication on the South Gate of the Tetragonos Agora, Ephesus, 4/3 BCE
properties.image_credit: Inscription on the Mazeus-Mithridates Gate, Ephesus — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Miletus
properties.one_line: Gnaeus Vergilius Capito, procurator of Asia under Claudius, gave Miletus a full Roman bath complex with a colonnaded court and an open-air swimming pool. His building inscription runs along the Ionic stoa that served as the entrance hall. Two colonnaded storeys curved around the bathing rooms, an ambitious piece of design for a provincial gift. Milesians were still bathing in it in 117 CE.
sources: Building inscription of the Ionic stoa fronting the Capito Baths, Miletus, c. 47-54 CE
properties.image_credit: Theatre of Miletus · Wikimedia Commons (reused, same site as mint_miletus)

properties.name: Leptis Magna
properties.one_line: Iddibal Caphada Aemilius, son of Himilis, paid for the Chalcidicum at Lepcis Magna — a colonnaded market hall with its own gateway and street — and dedicated it to the divine power of Augustus in 11-12 CE. The inscription across three gables names him alone as the man who covered the cost. A local Punic family, not Rome, put up the money. The complex still traded beside the theatre in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Market (Macellum) of Leptis Magna — Wikimedia Commons (reused, same site as euerg_lepcis_magna_market)

properties.name: Merida
properties.one_line: Marcus Agrippa gave the new colony of Augusta Emerita its theatre in 16-15 BCE and put his own name over the entrance passages. About 6,000 spectators sat in the tiered cavea cut into the hillside. The marble and granite stage front was rebuilt under Trajan, so the facade standing in 117 CE was barely a decade old. Emerita's citizens watched plays in a building paid for by the emperor's son-in-law.
sources: Building inscription 'M. Agrippa L.f. cos III trib. pot. III' over the theatre entrances, Augusta Emerita
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre of Merida — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Athens
properties.one_line: Marcus Agrippa dropped a covered concert hall into the middle of the Athenian Agora around 15 BCE, on ground that had stood deliberately open for four centuries. The two-storey auditorium seated roughly 1,000 and had a raised stage and a marble-paved orchestra. Athenians called it the Agrippeion after the man who paid. It was still hosting lectures and recitals in 117 CE.
sources: Athenian Agora excavations, Odeion of Agrippa (ASCSA)
properties.image_credit: Odeon of Agrippa, Athenian Agora — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Assisi
properties.one_line: Two brothers, Gnaeus Caesius and Titus Caesius Priscus, paid for the temple that still fronts Assisi's main square while serving as the town's chief magistrates. Six Corinthian columns rise straight off the stepped podium, an unusual arrangement forced by the cramped hillside terrace. Their dedication was spelled out in bronze letters across the architrave, and only the fixing holes now survive. The temple stood complete in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Minerva, Assisi — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Pula
properties.one_line: Salvia Postuma Sergia paid for the arch that still stands at Pula's Golden Gate, raising it to three dead Sergii — among them Lucius Sergius Lepidus, tribune of the 29th legion that fought at Actium. She put her own name on the frieze, a bold claim for a woman around 27 BCE. The arch was built against the inside of the city wall, so only its front face was ever meant to be seen. It stood in 117 CE and stands today.
sources: Dedicatory inscription of Salvia Postuma Sergia on the architrave of the Arch of the Sergii, Pula
properties.image_credit: Inscription, Arch of the Sergii, Pula — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Saintes
properties.one_line: Gaius Julius Rufus, a Gaulish notable and third-generation Roman citizen, paid for the twin-bayed arch at Saintes in 18-19 CE and dedicated it to Tiberius, Germanicus and Drusus. The inscription traces his line back to a grandfather named Gedemo, a Gaul who took the citizenship a lifetime earlier. The arch stood over the terminus of the road from Lyon, where travellers entered the town. It still framed that crossing in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Arc de Germanicus, Saintes — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5

properties.name: Lyon
properties.one_line: Gaius Julius Rufus of the Santones paid for the amphitheatre at the federal sanctuary of the Three Gauls in 19 CE, where delegates of sixty Gallic communities assembled each year. His dedication, made for the safety of Tiberius, turned up on a single reused block in 1957 and identified the whole building. The arena was enlarged a century after he built it. In 117 CE Rufus's amphitheatre was still the assembly's arena.
properties.image_credit: Amphitheatre of the Three Gauls, Lyon — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Pompeii
properties.one_line: Gaius Quinctius Valgus and Marcus Porcius, the colony's own duumvirs, built Pompeii's amphitheatre at their own expense around 70 BCE and handed the ground over to the colonists for good. Two copies of their dedication stood over its entrances -- it is the oldest stone amphitheatre known anywhere in the Roman world, built more than a century before the Colosseum.
properties.image_credit: Amphitheatre of Pompeii · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Pompeii
properties.one_line: The brothers Marcus Holconius Rufus and Marcus Holconius Celer paid to rebuild Pompeii's Large Theatre under Augustus, adding a whole new upper tier of seating on vaulted arcades and two private boxes flanking the stage. Twin inscriptions over six metres long, set into the stage building, made sure nobody who sat there forgot whose money it was.
properties.image_credit: Teatro Grande, Pompeii · Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

properties.name: Beneventum
properties.one_line: Trajan raised a monumental arch here in 114 CE to mark the completion of his new Via Traiana, and had masons carve the alimenta program into permanent public view inside its passage — the emperor handing out food money to children while personified Italian cities look on. The arch still spans the old road into town, its 26 sculpted panels the best-preserved visual record of how the welfare scheme actually looked in practice. Beneventum stood where the old Via Appia met Trajan's new coastal shortcut, making it the obvious place to put the emperor's signature program on permanent display for every traveler heading south.
sources: Arch of Trajan, Benevento, dedicated 114 CE — institutio alimentaria relief, inner attic passage
M. Rotili, L'arco di Traiano a Benevento (Rome, 1972)
properties.image_credit: Institutio Alimentaria relief, Arch of Trajan, Benevento — photo by Carole Raddato, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Piacenza
properties.one_line: Trajan's alimenta program reached this Po Valley colony directly, one of the string of Italian towns whose councils posted bronze tablets naming every child fed on the scheme's interest payments. Placentia's own farmland, some of it recorded on the neighboring Veleia tablet, backed part of the same mortgage-loan network. The colony had already stood here since 218 BCE, long before Trajan turned its fields into a welfare fund.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)

properties.name: Gubbio
properties.one_line: Gubbio's Roman town, terraced below the older Umbrian hill sanctuary that produced the bronze Iguvine Tablets, appears among the towns named in the surviving epigraphic record of Trajan's welfare program. Its council administered interest from mortgaged local farms as a monthly food stipend for freeborn children, the same mechanism recorded in exhaustive detail at nearby Veleia. A theatre built to seat nearly 6,000 still stands at the edge of the modern town.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)

properties.name: Libarna
properties.one_line: This small Ligurian colony on the road linking Genoa to the Po plain appears among the towns whose farmland was mortgaged into Trajan's alimenta network. Its amphitheater, theater, and street grid are still visible today near Serravalle Scrivia, evidence that this was a working Roman town and not just a name on a bronze tablet.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)

properties.name: Fermo
properties.one_line: Firmum Picenum's alimentary children set up a public dedication to the emperor after their food subsidy continued into a new reign. Free-born boys and girls of the town, called pueri et puellae alimentarii, inscribed their thanks on stone around 162 CE. The gift was funded by interest on state loans to local landowners, part of Trajan's Italy-wide child welfare program. Their monument survived to join a small set of similar dedications from across peninsular Italy.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, 'The Purpose and Organisation of the Alimenta', Papers of the British School at Rome 32 (1964), 123-146
properties.image_credit: Piazza del Popolo, historic center of Fermo (ancient Firmum Picenum) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Ostia
properties.one_line: Ostia ran its own local alimenta fund under a dedicated magistrate. The port town's cursus honorum lists a citizen, Marcus Antonius Severus, who served as quaestor alimentorum, the officer who controlled the special fund supporting poor children, alongside his duties as duovir and quaestor aerarii. The office shows Trajan's welfare scheme was administered as ordinary town business, run by local elected officials rather than solely by imperial appointees.
properties.image_credit: A surviving Latin epigraph among the ruins of Ostia Antica · Wikimedia Commons
